title: Persian Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: Zoroastrian scripture and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh mapped as one relationship graph: the two spirits and the Amesha Spentas, the bridge where your own conscience meets you, and the kings and heroes the epic made of them.

profile.cosmicNature: A war with a deadline. Two spirits existed at the start, one good and one destructive, and everything that happens is that fight working itself out over twelve thousand years. Unlike almost every other system here, this one ends - and it ends well. Evil is not eternal, it is temporary, and it loses. The world is not an illusion or a punishment; it is the good creation, invaded.
profile.natureOfDivinity: One god, and a staff. Ahura Mazda is the wise lord who created everything good, and around him stand six Amesha Spentas who are simultaneously archangels and abstractions - Good Purpose, Best Truth, Desirable Dominion, Holy Devotion, Wholeness, Immortality. Below them a crowd of yazatas, beings worthy of worship, several of whom are older Indo-Iranian gods kept on staff: Mithra, Anahita, Verethragna.
profile.afterlife: You are judged at a bridge, and the bridge changes width. Three days after death your soul comes to the Chinvat Bridge, where your own deeds meet you as a girl - beautiful if you lived well, hideous if you did not. For the good the bridge is broad and easy. For the wicked it narrows to a blade and they fall. But not forever: at the end everyone, including the damned, is purified in molten metal and restored.
profile.systemMechanism: Choose, and choose actively. The whole ethical system is three words - good thoughts, good words, good deeds - and the point is that a human being's choices are a real contribution to the outcome of the war. Farming, having children, keeping your word, killing vermin: these are all on the good side of the ledger. Asceticism is not a virtue here. Fasting is discouraged. Being useful is the religion.
profile.canonTexts: The Avesta - the Gathas attributed to Zarathustra himself, the Yasna, the Yashts and the Vendidad; the Pahlavi books, especially the Bundahishn, which is where the creation account is set out in full; and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, a poem of some fifty thousand couplets that saved the Persian language and the old stories together.

hierarchy.title: The Two Spirits
hierarchy.blurb: Not a creation from nothing but a war with a start date. One spirit made everything good; the other can only spoil it. The whole system is that fight, and it is scheduled to end - with the good side winning.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Around the Wise Lord stand six beings who are simultaneously virtues and things

hierarchy.title: The Amesha Spentas
hierarchy.blurb: Six Bounteous Immortals, each an abstract quality and a physical creation at once: Good Purpose has cattle, Best Truth has fire, Holy Devotion is the earth you stand on.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Below them, the yazatas - several of them older gods kept on the payroll

hierarchy.title: The Yazatas
hierarchy.blurb: Beings worthy of worship. Mithra is the contract itself, Anahita the world river, Tishtrya the star that fights for rain. Some are older than Zoroastrianism and were too useful to demote.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Against them, everything the Destructive Spirit could counterfeit

hierarchy.title: The Daevas
hierarchy.blurb: Wrath, Greed, the Lie, the corpse fly, drought and the demon who is death itself. None of them create anything; each is a spoiling of something that already worked.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: The war is fought over a world with a first man, a first ox and a first couple in it

hierarchy.title: The First Creation
hierarchy.blurb: A bright first man whose body became the metals, an ox whose death produced every useful plant and animal, and a first couple who grew as a rhubarb plant and lied within a month.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: A thousand years later a poet took the same figures and made them kings

hierarchy.title: The Shahnameh: the First Kings
hierarchy.blurb: Fire discovered by a thrown stone, demons made to teach writing, three hundred years of paradise ended by one boast - and then a tyrant with serpents growing out of his shoulders.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: A brother is murdered over an inheritance, and the war lasts the rest of the poem

hierarchy.title: The House of Sam
hierarchy.blurb: A champion abandons his albino son, a giant bird raises him, and the boy grows up to father the greatest hero in Persian literature - who kills his own son at a ford without knowing him.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: They serve kings who are, with one exception, not worth serving

hierarchy.title: Kings, Turan and the End
hierarchy.blurb: A king who tried to fly to heaven on eagles, a prince who rode through fire to prove his innocence and was murdered anyway, the one just king in the poem - and Iran's great enemy, given more depth than most of its heroes.

stories.title: The Two Spirits Choose
stories.summary: The oldest hymn in the book describes two spirits meeting at the beginning, twins in thought and word and deed, one good and one bad. They choose. One takes life, truth and the good creation; the other takes non-life and the Lie, and the daevas choose wrong along with him. This is the passage the entire religion rests on and the one nobody agrees about: is Spenta Mainyu the good god himself, which keeps it monotheist, or his brother, with Ahura Mazda above them both? Zoroastrian tradition took the first answer. What is not ambiguous is the consequence - evil is a choice something made, not something the good god built.

stories.title: Ahriman Attacks the World
stories.summary: Ohrmazd creates the world in six stages - sky, water, earth, plants, the sole-created ox, and the first man - and holds it perfect and motionless for three thousand years. Then Ahriman breaks in through the base of the sky. He fouls the water with salt, drives winter into the earth, withers the plants, kills the ox and kills Gayomard. But he is trapped inside: the sky closes behind him like a fortress with the enemy shut in, and he must fight there until he is destroyed. Ohrmazd's counter-attack knocks him senseless for three thousand years, and the demons cannot rouse him until Jahi promises to ruin everything he made.

sources.book: The Bundahishn (Sacred Books of the East V)

stories.title: The Ox, the Man and the Metals
stories.summary: Both first creatures die in the assault, and both deaths are productive. From the ox come fifty-five grains and twelve healing plants; its seed goes up to the moon, is purified there, and becomes every beneficial animal species. Gayomard holds out thirty years and his body yields the seven metals - gold from his seed, which is purified in the sun for forty years and grows as a rhubarb plant with fifteen leaves. The plant becomes Mashya and Mashyana, so joined that it was not clear which was which. They are told they are human, to think and speak and act well, and not to worship demons. It takes them about thirty days to get it wrong.

sources.book: The Bundahishn (Sacred Books of the East V)

stories.title: The Soul of the Ox Files a Complaint
stories.summary: The soul of the murdered ox goes up and cries out: for whom was I made, who appointed a protector for me, why am I given over to violence and cruelty? Asha answers that there is no herdsman on earth free of sin. The soul demands someone with power to help. Ahura Mazda names Zarathustra, a man who has learned the words. The soul is openly disappointed - it wanted a mighty prince and has been offered someone with, it says, a feeble voice - and accepts him grudgingly. It is one of the oldest passages in the corpus and it opens the founding scripture of the religion with livestock lodging a grievance and finding the response inadequate.

sources.book: The Yasna and the Gathas (Sacred Books of the East XXXI)

stories.title: The Rain-Star Fights the Drought
stories.summary: Tishtrya goes down to the cosmic sea as a white stallion with golden ears and golden trappings, and Apaosha meets him as a black horse, bald, with no hair on ears or tail. They fight three days and nights and the drought demon wins, driving the star back a full league from the water. Tishtrya cries out to Ahura Mazda that he has not the strength because people have not sacrificed to him and named him in worship. He is given the strength of ten horses, ten camels, ten bulls, ten mountains and ten rivers, comes back, drives Apaosha off, and the waters go out over the earth. The bargain between people and gods has rarely been put so plainly.

sources.book: The Zend-Avesta (Sacred Books of the East IV, XXIII)

stories.title: The Bridge and the Girl
stories.summary: For three days after death the soul stays near the body. On the dawn of the fourth it goes to the Chinvat Bridge, where Mithra, Sraosha and Rashnu wait with golden scales. A wind meets it, and a young woman. If the life was good she is fifteen years old and more beautiful than anything the soul has seen, and she says: I am your own conscience, I was lovely and your good thoughts and words and deeds made me lovelier. The bridge widens to nine spears and she leads the way across. If the life was bad the same figure meets the soul as a hag, says the same words in reverse, and the bridge narrows to a razor's edge.

stories.title: The Making Wonderful
stories.summary: At the end of twelve thousand years the last saviour is born to a virgin who bathes in the lake where Zarathustra's seed has been kept. Azhi Dahaka breaks his chains and destroys a third of everything before he is killed. The dead are raised, body and soul reunited. All the metal in the mountains melts into a river and everyone passes through it - to the righteous it feels like warm milk, and the wicked are burned, but the burning takes the evil out of them rather than destroying them. Then Ahriman is finished, and everyone, including those who were in hell, goes on into a world made new and deathless. Nobody is left behind.

sources.book: The Bundahishn (Sacred Books of the East V)

stories.title: The Prophet Is Called
stories.summary: At thirty Zarathustra goes to draw water for a spring festival and wades out to where the stream runs pure. Coming up the bank he sees Vohu Manah, Good Purpose, nine times the height of a man, who asks who he is and what he most wants in life, and takes him to the assembly of Ahura Mazda. He preaches for ten years and converts one person, his cousin. Then he reaches the court of Vishtaspa, is framed by jealous priests who plant unclean things in his lodging, and is imprisoned - until the king's favourite horse has its legs drawn up into its body, and Zarathustra offers to cure it one leg at a time in exchange for four things.

stories.title: Jamshid Loses the Glory
stories.summary: Jamshid's three hundred years are the golden age - classes established, weaving, medicine, ships, mining, perfume, and death itself abolished. He founds Nowruz by having demons carry his throne into the sky on the first day of spring, and the world looks up at him. Then he calls the assembly and tells them he is god, and that they should worship no one else. The royal glory leaves him in three flights, in the form of a bird. His nobles turn to the serpent-shouldered Zahhak, who invades. Jamshid runs for a hundred years, is caught at last by the sea, and is sawn in half. Everything he built survives him; the reign is remembered as both the best and the cautionary one.

stories.title: The Blacksmith's Apron
stories.summary: Zahhak rules a thousand years and two young men are killed every day to feed the serpents on his shoulders. Kaveh the blacksmith has lost seventeen sons to them. When the officers come for the eighteenth he goes to the palace, where the king is circulating a document for the nobles to sign attesting that he has always ruled with justice. Kaveh reads it aloud, denounces it in front of the whole court, tears it up and walks out with his son. In the street he raises his leather apron on the point of a spear, and people follow him. Fereydun takes the throne with that mob behind him, and the apron becomes the royal standard of Iran for a thousand years.

stories.title: The Division of the World
stories.summary: Fereydun divides the world between his three sons: Rome and the west to Salm, Turan and China to Tur, and Iran - the middle and the best - to the youngest, Iraj. The two elder brothers demand that Iraj be disinherited. Iraj goes to them alone and unarmed and offers to give up the throne entirely rather than have a war over it, and Tur kills him with a golden stool and then a dagger, and they send the head back to their father in a box. Fereydun's grief takes up pages. Iraj's grandson Manuchehr eventually kills them both and returns two heads. Iran is named after Iraj, Turan after Tur, and the feud runs the rest of the poem.

stories.title: The Bird Who Raised a Child
stories.summary: Sam's son is born perfect except for white hair, and Sam - afraid of being laughed at - has him left on the Alborz to die. The Simurgh takes the baby to her nest and raises him with her own young. Years later Sam dreams of him and rides out, and finds a young man on the mountain. The bird gives him back and leaves three feathers: burn one and she will come. Zal uses two of them. The first is for Rudabeh, who cannot deliver their child - the Simurgh arrives and dictates the procedure, wine for the pain, an incision in the side, the baby lifted out, and a herb rubbed on the wound. The child is Rostam.

stories.title: The Seven Trials of Rostam
stories.summary: Kay Kavus invades Mazandaran on a demon's advice, and the White Demon blinds him and his whole army and locks them up. Rostam goes after them alone. A lion attacks while he sleeps and Rakhsh kills it without waking him, and gets scolded for the risk. He nearly dies of thirst and the horse finds water. He kills a dragon that is invisible each time he looks, and a sorceress who comes as a beautiful woman and turns black when he says a holy name. At the last he finds the White Demon asleep in a cave, wakes it rather than strike a sleeping enemy, tears off a leg, and takes its liver - the blood of which restores the army's sight.

stories.title: Rostam and Sohrab
stories.summary: Tahmineh sends Rostam word that their child was a girl, so that he will not be taken away for war. Sohrab grows up enormous, learns who his father is, and marches on Iran meaning to put Rostam on the throne. At the White Castle he is fought to a standstill by Gordafarid in armour. At the Iranian camp the two champions meet and neither knows the other. Sohrab asks twice whether he is Rostam and is told no. On the first day Sohrab throws him and spares him; on the second Rostam throws Sohrab and stabs him at once, and then sees the onyx armlet. He sends to Kay Kavus for the healing elixir. The king refuses it, and the boy dies.

stories.title: Siyavash Rides Through the Fire
stories.summary: Sudabeh, his stepmother, has Siyavash brought to the women's quarters, propositions him, and is refused. She tears her clothes and accuses him. To settle it two mountains of wood are built and set alight, and Siyavash rides between them on a black horse and comes out the far side with his clothes unmarked. His father, who has watched this, still cannot be relied on. Ordered later to break a treaty he has sworn to, Siyavash refuses and goes into exile in Turan instead, where Afrasiyab receives him as a son and marries him to his daughter - and then, worked on by slander, has him beheaded. A plant grows where the blood fell.

stories.title: Bizhan in the Pit
stories.summary: Bizhan crosses into Turan and meets Manizheh, Afrasiyab's daughter, at a festival; she drugs him and has him carried into her father's palace. When they are found the king throws Bizhan into a pit and seals it with an enormous stone, and strips Manizheh of everything and drives her out. She begs in the streets for months and passes food down to him through a gap. Kay Khosrow locates him in the world-revealing cup, and Rostam goes into Turan disguised as a merchant. Manizheh knows him when he drops a ring into her water jug. Rostam lifts the stone alone, and they take her back to Iran with them and receive her honourably.

stories.title: Rostam and Esfandiyar
stories.summary: Goshtasp has promised his son the throne repeatedly and each time found one more task first. The last is to bring Rostam to court in chains. Both men know the order is unjust and neither can refuse it - Esfandiyar because a son obeys, Rostam because he will not be chained. They talk for a long time before they fight, each trying to find a way out. Then they fight, and Rostam cannot wound him, because Zarathustra made him invulnerable. Wounded and losing, Rostam burns a Simurgh feather. The bird tells him to find a tamarisk by the sea, cut a double-headed arrow, and aim for the eyes, which were shut when the blessing was given.

stories.title: The King Who Walked Away
stories.summary: Kay Khosrow finishes the war his grandfather started. He hunts Afrasiyab down at last, avenges his father Siyavash, and stands at the head of an undefeated empire with the royal glory visibly on him. Then he stops. He tells his nobles he has been thinking about Jamshid, who had everything and let it turn him, and that he does not trust himself to hold this much and stay just. He names a successor, distributes his treasure, takes formal leave of everyone, and walks up into the mountains. Several of his companions follow and are lost in a snowstorm. The poem does not say he died. It simply stops following him.
