entities.name: Ahura Mazda
entities.role: The Wise Lord, who made everything good and is winning slowly
symbols: the winged disc of the Faravahar
entities.bio: The one god - wise rather than almighty, which is the whole point of the system.
entities.longBio: Ahura Mazda made everything good: the sky, water, earth, plants, animals, people, and fire. What he did not make is evil, and that is deliberate. Zoroastrianism's answer to why a good god permits suffering is that he does not - there is a second spirit doing it, and the good god is not yet in full control. He is called wise rather than all-powerful, and the war is real. His symbol is fire, kept burning in temples for centuries at a time, and Iranian kings from Darius onward credited him personally with their thrones.
entities.variantTraditions: The Gathas present him as sole creator with Spenta Mainyu as his own bounteous spirit; later Zurvanite tradition made him and Ahriman twin sons of Time, which mainstream Zoroastrianism rejects.

entities.name: Angra Mainyu
entities.role: The Destructive Spirit, who invented death and cannot invent anything else
entities.bio: He can only spoil what already exists - every evil is a counterfeit of something good.
entities.longBio: Angra Mainyu is not a rebel angel and not a tempter; he is a separate origin, coeternal at the start, whose entire method is ruination. He cannot create. Everything he produces is a corruption of an existing good thing - Ahura Mazda makes life, he makes death; makes health, he makes disease; makes summer, he makes winter. He attacks the world at the beginning, is trapped inside it, and thrashes about for nine thousand years. At the end he is defeated absolutely and destroyed, which is the crucial difference from later devils: he is temporary.
entities.variantTraditions: Ahriman is the Middle Persian form. The Zoroastrian solution to evil - a second uncreated principle - is the origin of the word dualism as used in religious studies.

entities.name: Zurvan
entities.role: Infinite Time, who sacrificed for a son and got two
entities.bio: A heretical answer to an awkward question: if good and evil are twins, who was their father?
entities.longBio: Zurvan is Time, and he belongs to a branch of Zoroastrianism that mainstream priests rejected. The story: Zurvan sacrificed for a thousand years wanting a son, then doubted for a moment - and got two, Ohrmazd from the sacrifice and Ahriman from the doubt. He had promised the kingship to whichever came first, and Ahriman tore his way out early to claim it, so Zurvan gave him nine thousand years and Ohrmazd everything after. It is a neat fix for the problem of where the two spirits came from, and orthodox Zoroastrianism has always regarded it as a mistake.
entities.variantTraditions: Zurvanism is known largely from hostile Christian and Manichaean reports and from a few Pahlavi passages; how widespread it was under the Sasanians is disputed.

entities.name: Spenta Mainyu
entities.role: The Bounteous Spirit - Ahura Mazda's own creative energy, or his twin
entities.bio: Whether he is the good god himself or the good god's active spirit is the oldest argument in the religion.
entities.longBio: In the Gathas, two spirits meet at the beginning and choose - one takes life and truth, the other non-life and the lie. Spenta Mainyu is the one who chooses well. The problem is what he is: read one way he is Ahura Mazda's own creative aspect, the way the god acts in the world, which keeps the system monotheistic. Read another he is a twin brother of Angra Mainyu, with Ahura Mazda above both. Zoroastrian tradition took the first reading and later collapsed the two together entirely.
entities.variantTraditions: The interpretation of Yasna 30, the twin-spirits hymn, is the single most contested passage in Zoroastrian scholarship.

entities.name: Vohu Manah
entities.role: Good Purpose, who guards cattle and met Zarathustra first
entities.bio: The first of the six, and the one who came to fetch Zarathustra when the revelation started.
entities.longBio: Vohu Manah is Good Purpose - the settled intention to do right, as opposed to a passing good mood - and he is the highest of the Amesha Spentas. He is also the one who appears at the beginning of the prophet's career: Zarathustra, aged thirty, comes up from a river at a spring festival and Vohu Manah is standing there, nine times a man's height, and takes him to Ahura Mazda. He looks after cattle, which in a herding society is not a minor portfolio, and he greets the righteous soul in paradise and shows it to a seat.
entities.variantTraditions: Each Amesha Spenta guards one of the seven creations. Vohu Manah has cattle; the pairing of abstract virtue with concrete stuff runs through the whole set.

entities.name: Asha Vahishta
entities.role: Best Truth: the order of the universe, and the guardian of fire
entities.bio: Not honesty - the correct working of everything, from the seasons to a promise kept.
entities.longBio: Asha is the largest idea in the religion and the hardest to translate. It is truth, rightness, and the order by which the world actually functions, all at once; its opposite, Druj, is the Lie in the same expanded sense - disorder, falsehood, and everything out of joint. Asha Vahishta is Best Truth personified, and his creation is fire, which is why fire sits at the centre of every temple. The word is cognate with Sanskrit rta, the cosmic order of the Vedas, which puts it among the oldest religious concepts anyone has written down.
entities.variantTraditions: Asha, Vedic rta and possibly Greek arete descend from a shared Indo-European root. Fire is not worshipped in Zoroastrianism; it is faced, as the visible form of Asha.

entities.name: Khshathra Vairya
entities.role: Desirable Dominion: the kingdom worth having, and the guardian of metal
entities.bio: The power that ought to be, rather than the power that is - and he owns all the metal.
entities.longBio: Khshathra Vairya is dominion as it should be exercised: rule that protects rather than exploits, which the texts tie directly to defending the weak. His creation is metal, and that connects to the end of the world - at the Frashokereti all metal in the mountains melts into a river that everyone must cross. To the righteous it feels like warm milk; to the wicked it burns, but it burns the evil out of them rather than destroying them, and afterwards everyone continues. A god of both kingship and molten metal is not a coincidence.
entities.variantTraditions: The molten-metal ordeal is the mechanism of universal salvation in Zoroastrianism: punishment is corrective and finite, not eternal.

entities.name: Spenta Armaiti
entities.role: Holy Devotion, who is also the earth you are standing on
entities.bio: Devotion personified, and the ground - which is why polluting the earth is a religious offence.
entities.longBio: Spenta Armaiti is the settled loyal devotion of a person who serves willingly, and she is the earth. The identification is not decorative: because the earth is a holy being, burying a corpse in it is a serious pollution, which is why Zoroastrians exposed their dead on towers instead. Farming, irrigating and cultivating are acts of piety toward her. In the Gathas she is Ahura Mazda's daughter, and she is the Amesha Spenta most often invoked in ordinary domestic life.
entities.variantTraditions: The prohibition on burial follows directly from her identification with the earth, together with the corpse demon Nasu.

entities.name: Haurvatat
entities.role: Wholeness, who guards the waters
entities.bio: Health in the largest sense - being entire and unbroken - and all the water in the world.
entities.longBio: Haurvatat is wholeness: physical health, but more broadly the state of being complete and undamaged, which is what the good creation was before it was attacked. Her creation is water. She goes everywhere with Ameretat, Immortality, and the pair are almost never named separately - wholeness and deathlessness are what a person gets at the end, and what the world gets back at the renovation. Her name is related to Sanskrit sarvatat, and the pairing survives, oddly, into the Islamic angels Harut and Marut.
entities.variantTraditions: The identification of Harut and Marut in the Quran with Haurvatat and Ameretat is widely accepted by scholars though the two figures behave very differently.

entities.name: Ameretat
entities.role: Immortality, who guards plants
entities.bio: Deathlessness, in charge of vegetation - because plants come back and that is the proof.
entities.longBio: Ameretat is immortality, the condition the world will be restored to, and her creation is plants. The logic is agricultural: vegetation dies back and returns, which is deathlessness demonstrated annually. She and Haurvatat travel as a pair. At the renovation of the world, the saviour prepares a drink from the fat of a sacred bull and white haoma, and everyone who takes it becomes immortal - Ameretat's portfolio delivered. The Iranian month Amordad and the Persian name Mordad both come from her.
entities.variantTraditions: Six Amesha Spentas plus Ahura Mazda make seven, and each holds one of the seven creations - sky, water, earth, plants, cattle, humanity and fire.

entities.name: Mithra
entities.role: God of the contract, who has a thousand ears and never blinks
entities.abode: The peak of Hara, ahead of the sun
entities.bio: Break a promise and he comes for you - which is why every deal in Iran was sworn on his name.
entities.longBio: Mithra is the contract itself, made into a god. The great hymn to him says he has a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes, never sleeps, and rides ahead of the sunrise over the mountains to see whether anyone has broken faith. A man who lies to a contract-partner ruins his whole country. He is old - the same god as Vedic Mitra, and named in a Hittite treaty from 1400 BC - and he outlasted Zoroastrianism's attempt to demote him. Later, and quite separately, a Roman mystery cult built itself around a figure called Mithras who kills a bull.
entities.variantTraditions: The relationship between Iranian Mithra and Roman Mithras is disputed. The Roman cult's central image, the bull-killing, has no Iranian counterpart at all.

entities.name: Anahita
entities.role: Goddess of the waters, who wears beaver furs and grants nothing to the wicked
symbols: the golden crown with eight rays
entities.abode: Mount Hara, from which all waters flow
entities.bio: Every hero asks her for a favour, and she refuses the ones who do not deserve it.
entities.longBio: Anahita is the world river, pouring off the mythical mountain into the sea, and the source of all fresh water and fertility. Her hymn describes her physically in unusual detail - a tall strong woman in a gold-embroidered mantle and beaver furs, with a jewelled crown. The structure of the hymn is a queue: hero after hero sacrifices a hundred horses and a thousand cattle and asks for something, and she grants it - except to Azhi Dahaka and Afrasiyab, who ask for the same power and are refused. Artaxerxes II put up statues of her, which was a scandal.
entities.variantTraditions: Her cult absorbed Mesopotamian Ishtar material under the Achaemenids, and the statue-building marks a real break with earlier Iranian aniconism.

entities.name: Verethragna
entities.role: Victory, who shows up in ten different bodies including a boar and a strong wind
entities.bio: Ten incarnations, and the best of them is a wild boar that comes through the ranks sideways.
entities.longBio: Verethragna is the smashing of resistance rather than victory in the abstract, and his hymn lists ten forms he takes: a wind, a bull with gold horns, a white horse, a rutting camel, a boar, a fifteen-year-old youth, a raven, a ram, a buck, and an armed man. The boar is the most vividly described - sharp-tusked, killing at one stroke, working itself into a fury. He is the same word as Vedic Vritrahan, the epithet of Indra, so the name is older than the religion. He gives strength to the arm and health to the body, and the Sasanian kings named themselves after him.
entities.variantTraditions: Bahram is the later Persian form, and the name is common as both a royal name and, via the fire-temple grade Bahram, a fire classification.

entities.name: Sraosha
entities.role: Obedience: the only god who stays awake all night guarding the world
symbols: the house on Hara with a thousand pillars
entities.bio: The demons come out at night, so he does not sleep - and the rooster is his herald.
entities.longBio: Sraosha means hearing or obedience, and he is what happens when you listen to what the religion tells you. His job is practical: he patrols the world from sunset onward with a raised mace, because that is when the daevas move. The cockerel is his bird, calling people to get up and pray and driving off the demon of sloth, and killing one is a sin. He is one of the three judges at the Chinvat Bridge with Mithra and Rashnu, and he escorts the righteous soul across. He is also the last thing the dying hear about.
entities.variantTraditions: Sraosha is the only yazata who receives a full liturgy of his own. The connection between a god of obedience and a rooster is drawn explicitly in the Vendidad.

entities.name: Rashnu
entities.role: The judge, who holds the scales at the bridge and cannot be bribed
entities.bio: He weighs your deeds on golden scales, and the texts stress he does not favour anyone.
entities.longBio: Rashnu stands at the Chinvat Bridge with a pair of golden scales and weighs the soul's good deeds against the bad. He is described as absolutely impartial: he does not favour the rich, the strong or the well-connected, and the texts return to this point often enough that one suspects earthly judges of the period did. He also presided over ordeals in the living world, where an accused person swore an oath or underwent a physical test in his name. With Mithra and Sraosha he makes the tribunal of three.
entities.variantTraditions: The weighing of deeds at a bridge influenced later Islamic imagery of the Sirat bridge, though how directly is argued.

entities.name: Tishtrya
entities.role: The star Sirius, who fights the drought demon as a white horse and loses the first round
symbols: the white stallion with gold ears
entities.abode: The sky, and the shore of the cosmic sea
entities.bio: He fights for rain in the shape of a white horse, and how much sacrifice he gets decides whether he wins.
entities.longBio: Tishtrya is Sirius, and his hymn is one of the most exciting things in the Avesta. He goes down to the cosmic sea in the form of a white stallion with golden ears to make rain, and the drought demon Apaosha meets him as a black horse with no hair. They fight for three days and nights and Apaosha wins, driving him back - because, Tishtrya complains to Ahura Mazda, people have not sacrificed to him and he has not got the strength. Given a proper sacrifice he returns with the strength of ten horses, drives Apaosha off, and the water comes. The bargain is stated with unusual bluntness.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tir festival Tiregan is still kept, and the star's heliacal rising marked the start of the rains in the Iranian year.

entities.name: Atar
entities.role: Fire, the son of Ahura Mazda, who once wrestled a dragon for the royal glory
entities.bio: Not a symbol of the god but a being in his own right - and he fought Azhi Dahaka personally.
entities.longBio: Atar is fire as a person, called the son of Ahura Mazda, and Zoroastrians pray facing him rather than to him. Temple fires are graded, and the highest, the Atash Behram, is assembled from sixteen different fires including one caused by lightning and one from a cremation pyre, then purified over about a year. Some have burned continuously for over a thousand years. In myth he has a real fight: when Azhi Dahaka grabs at the khvarenah, the royal glory, Atar goes after it too, and the dragon threatens to put him out while he threatens to burn its mouth.
entities.variantTraditions: The label fire-worshipper is a persistent and resented mischaracterisation; fire is the visible sign of Asha and the direction of prayer, not its object.

entities.name: Haoma
entities.role: A plant, a drink, and a god - who visits Zarathustra and asks to be pressed
epithets: the one who drives death far away
entities.bio: The god turns up in person and asks the prophet to press him - which is exactly as strange as it sounds.
entities.longBio: Haoma is simultaneously a plant, the drink pressed from it, and the god of both. His hymn opens with Zarathustra tending a fire at dawn when Haoma comes to him and asks to be pressed and praised, and then explains who has pressed him before and what each of them got. The drink is central to the Yasna liturgy and is still prepared. It is the same word and the same substance as Vedic soma, and what the original plant was has been argued about for two centuries - ephedra is the current favourite, opinions have included wild rue, mushrooms and cannabis.
entities.variantTraditions: Modern Zoroastrian practice uses ephedra. The Vedic soma and Iranian haoma are cognate, which puts the ritual before the two traditions separated.

entities.name: Vayu
entities.role: The wind, who works for both sides and is prayed to carefully
epithets: he who moves in both worlds
entities.abode: The space between sky and earth
entities.bio: There are two of him - a good wind and a bad one - and his hymn hedges the whole way through.
entities.longBio: Vayu is the wind and the empty space between heaven and earth, and he is genuinely ambiguous in a religion that does not usually permit that. Part of him belongs to Ahura Mazda and part to Angra Mainyu; one Vayu brings the breath of life and the other takes it away at death. His hymn addresses him with visible caution, praising the good part by name. Heroes sacrifice to him for favours and get them. He is the same god as Vedic Vayu, and this two-sidedness is very likely older than the sorting of the world into good and evil.
entities.variantTraditions: The good Vayu and bad Vayu are separated more firmly in the Pahlavi books than in the Avesta, which reads as later tidying-up.

entities.name: Ashi
entities.role: Fortune and reward, who complains that the wicked hide her from her own worshippers
entities.bio: Not luck - what you have earned, which the texts insist is a different thing.
entities.longBio: Ashi is the reward that follows right action, and specifically the material kind: cattle, crops, a full house, healthy children. She is the sister of Sraosha, Mithra's charioteer, and one of the few figures who gets an emotional moment - in her hymn she takes refuge under Zarathustra's chariot and complains bitterly about two kinds of people who cheat her, courtesans and men who do not father children, since neither produces the households she exists to fill. It is a startlingly practical grievance for a divine being.
entities.variantTraditions: The pairing of a reward goddess with a fertility complaint reflects Zoroastrianism's insistence that producing and sustaining life is a religious duty.

entities.name: Daena
entities.role: Your own conscience, who meets you after death wearing the face you gave her
entities.abode: The head of the Chinvat Bridge
entities.bio: The most vivid image in the religion: your soul meets a girl, and she looks exactly like your life.
entities.longBio: Three days after death the soul goes to the bridge and meets a young woman. If you lived well she is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen, fifteen years old, radiant, and she says: I am your own daena, your conscience - I was lovely and you made me lovelier. If you lived badly the same figure meets you as a hag so foul the soul recoils, and she says the same thing in reverse. She is not a judge and she does not punish. She is what you turned yourself into, standing in front of you.
entities.variantTraditions: Daena also means religion in the ordinary sense - the modern Persian din, and the same word borrowed into Arabic. The doubled meaning is not an accident.

entities.name: Hvare Khshaeta
entities.role: The visible sun, whose rising drives the demons out of the world every morning
entities.bio: When he comes up the daevas run, and that happens every single day.
entities.longBio: Hvare Khshaeta is the actual sun in the sky, distinct from Mithra, and his function is daily disinfection: when the sun rises the earth is made clean and the demons that gather in the dark are scattered. Where he does not shine, the texts say, the daevas destroy everything. He is called the eye of Ahura Mazda, and his light is one of the things a Zoroastrian prays facing. His name survives as Khorshid, still a common Persian given name, and the fourth watch of the day belongs to him.
entities.variantTraditions: The distinction between Hvare Khshaeta as the sun's disc and Mithra as the contract-god associated with sunrise blurs steadily in later texts.

entities.name: Mah
entities.role: The moon, who keeps the seed of the primordial bull
epithets: the one that holds the cattle seed
symbols: the bull's seed purified in moonlight
entities.bio: The moon holds the seed of the first bull, which is where every useful animal came from.
entities.longBio: Mah is the moon and, in the Zoroastrian scheme, a storage facility: when the primordial bull was killed, its seed was carried up to the moon, purified there, and from it came every species of beneficent animal. The moon's phases govern the calendar and the growth of plants, and the hymn addresses him as the one who keeps the seed of cattle. His portfolio is agricultural rather than romantic; there is nothing lunar-feminine about him, and he is male.
entities.variantTraditions: The bull's seed in the moon is from the Bundahishn rather than the Avesta, part of the fuller Pahlavi creation account.

entities.name: Aeshma
entities.role: Wrath, who carries a bloody club and became Asmodeus
entities.bio: The demon of rage, and one of the few figures here with a straight line into the Bible.
entities.longBio: Aeshma is fury - the loss of control that ends in violence - and he is the standing enemy of Sraosha, obedience. He rushes at cattle and at people with a bloody club, and the texts treat losing your temper as an actual invasion rather than a character flaw. The interesting part is where he ends up: Aeshma-daeva becomes Asmodeus in the Book of Tobit, the demon who kills seven bridegrooms, and later a duke of hell in medieval demonology. He is one of the clearest imports from Iranian religion into Jewish and Christian tradition.
entities.variantTraditions: The etymology Aeshma-daeva to Asmodeus is generally accepted, and Tobit is among the strongest evidence for Zoroastrian influence on Second Temple Judaism.

entities.name: Az
entities.role: Greed, who eats everything including, at the very end, herself
entities.bio: The demon of wanting more, who will devour the other demons when nothing else is left.
entities.longBio: Az is greed in the broad sense - appetite that cannot be satisfied, covering food, wealth and sex alike. She is described as swallowing everything, and when there is nothing left she starts on the demons themselves, and finally on Ahriman, which is one way of saying that evil consumes itself. Zoroastrian ethics is unusually blunt here: excessive fasting is a sin as well, because starving the body is Az winning from the other direction. Manichaeism took her over and made her considerably more central.
entities.variantTraditions: Az is more prominent in the Pahlavi books and in Manichaean texts than in the Avesta itself.

entities.name: Druj
entities.role: The Lie - not lying, but everything false and out of joint
entities.bio: The single word the whole religion is arranged against, and it means much more than dishonesty.
entities.longBio: Druj is the exact opposite of Asha, and like Asha it is bigger than its English translation. It is falsehood, but also disorder, corruption, and the state of things being wrong - a rotting corpse is druj, a broken contract is druj, and so is a lie. Human beings are sorted into ashavan, those who belong to Truth, and dregvant, those who belong to the Lie, and the choice is made in the ordinary business of living rather than in a moment of conversion. The word is cognate with English betray by way of a shared root meaning to deceive.
entities.variantTraditions: Druj is both an abstract principle and a class of female demons in the Vendidad, most importantly Nasu, the corpse demon.

entities.name: Nasu
entities.role: The corpse demon, who arrives as a fly the instant someone dies
symbols: the two dogs whose gaze drives her off
entities.bio: She comes in the shape of a fly from the north, and the whole Zoroastrian funeral is designed around her.
entities.longBio: The moment life leaves a body, Nasu rushes into it as a fly and the corpse becomes the most polluting thing there is. Everything about Zoroastrian death practice follows from this: bodies are not buried, because the earth is holy, and not burned, because fire is holy, so they are exposed on towers for the birds. She is driven back by the sagdid, the gaze of a dog - a four-eyed dog, meaning one with spots above the eyes, is led in to look at the body. Whatever the theology, it is also a strikingly good account of contagion.
entities.variantTraditions: The dog's importance in Zoroastrianism is unusual among Near Eastern religions, and killing one carries severe penalties in the Vendidad.

entities.name: Apaosha
entities.role: The drought demon, a black horse with no hair
entities.abode: The shore of the cosmic sea
entities.bio: He beat Tishtrya the first time, and in a country like Iran that is the worst news there is.
entities.longBio: Apaosha is drought as a person, and he appears in the shape of a black stallion, bald, with no hair on ears or tail. He meets Tishtrya at the cosmic sea and they fight for three days, and Apaosha wins the first bout and drives the rain-star back a full league. Only after a proper sacrifice does Tishtrya come back strong enough to beat him. In a land where the whole agricultural year depends on the rains arriving, making drought an enemy who can actually win the fight is a more honest theology than most.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tishtrya-Apaosha combat is the clearest surviving Iranian version of the widespread Indo-European storm-god versus withholding-demon pattern.

entities.name: Astvidatu
entities.role: The bone-divider: the demon who is the actual moment of death
domains: the separation of soul and body
symbols: the noose thrown around the neck
entities.abode: At the end of every life
entities.bio: He throws a noose over your neck at birth, and it stays there loose until it does not.
entities.longBio: Astvidatu is death itself rather than a god of the dead. He casts a noose around the neck of every person at birth; if they die righteous it falls away, and if not it drags them down. He is described as the one from whom no one escapes, including kings and heroes, and the Pahlavi texts stress that the strong and the clever fare no better. He works with Vayu, the wind that takes the breath. There is nothing negotiable about him, and no story in which anyone gets away.
entities.variantTraditions: The Menog-i Khrad devotes a passage to the impossibility of escaping him, which reads as a genuine attempt to console rather than to frighten.

entities.name: Jahi
entities.role: The demon who woke Ahriman up when he had lost the will to fight
epithets: the primal woman of the Lie
entities.bio: After three thousand years flattened, Ahriman was finished - and she got him back on his feet.
entities.longBio: When Ahriman first attacks the good creation, Ohrmazd's counter-attack knocks him unconscious for three thousand years, and the demons cannot rouse him. Jahi does it: she promises to ruin the righteous man, the fire, the water, the earth, the plants and everything else, and Ahriman rises, kisses her on the head, and menstruation appears in the world from that kiss. This passage is the source of the harshest treatment of women in the Zoroastrian corpus, and it sits badly beside a religion that elsewhere treats men and women as equally capable of choosing truth.
entities.variantTraditions: The Bundahishn passage is late and its misogyny is not characteristic of the Gathas, which address men and women together. It is reported here because it is in the text.

entities.name: Azhi Dahaka
entities.role: The three-headed dragon with six eyes, chained under a mountain until the end
entities.bio: The Avesta's dragon and the epic's tyrant are the same creature, and he is not dead - only chained.
entities.longBio: In the Avesta, Azhi Dahaka is a dragon with three mouths, three heads and six eyes, made by Angra Mainyu to ruin the world, and full of vermin - snakes, lizards and scorpions crawl in his body. Thraetaona fights him and does not kill him, because striking him open would release the vermin over the earth; instead he binds him inside Mount Damavand. At the end of the world he breaks loose, destroys a third of everything, and is finally killed by the resurrected hero Keresaspa. The Shahnameh keeps every beat and makes him a human king with serpents on his shoulders.
entities.variantTraditions: Damavand is a real volcano north-east of Tehran, and the tradition of the chained dragon inside it is still current in Iranian folklore.

entities.name: Gayomard
entities.role: The first man, shaped like a bright cylinder, whose body became metal
domains: the origin of the human race
entities.bio: He shone like the sun, lived thirty years after the attack, and when he died the metals came out of him.
entities.longBio: Gayomard is the first man, created bright and tall and shaped, the Bundahishn says, like the sun. Ahriman's assault kills him, but he holds out thirty years first, and as he dies his body yields the seven metals - gold from his seed, and the rest from his limbs. His seed is purified in the sun for forty years, and from it grows a rhubarb plant which becomes the first human couple. In the Shahnameh he is demoted to the first king instead, ruling from a mountain and dressed in leopard skins, and the metaphysics is dropped.
entities.variantTraditions: The name means mortal life. The transformation from cosmic first-man to first king is one of the clearest cases of the epic historicising scripture.

entities.name: Mashya and Mashyana
entities.role: The first couple, who grew as a rhubarb plant and lied within a month
symbols: the rhubarb plant with fifteen leaves
entities.bio: They grew out of the ground as one plant with fifteen leaves, and got it wrong almost immediately.
entities.longBio: Mashya and Mashyana grow from Gayomard's purified seed as a single rhubarb plant so joined that it was not clear which was which, and then become human. Ahura Mazda tells them they are people, to think good thoughts and do good deeds and not worship demons. They manage about thirty days. First they declare that Ahriman created the world, which is the first lie and costs them heaven. Then they lose the taste for food, kill a goat and roast it, quarrel, and go fifty years without children out of spite. Eventually they produce twins, and eat them.
entities.variantTraditions: The account is from the Bundahishn. The parallel with Genesis is often noted, but the sin here is a false statement about who made the world rather than disobedience.

entities.name: The Primordial Bull
entities.role: The uniquely created ox, from whose death every useful plant and animal came
domains: the origin of animals and plants
symbols: the moon that holds its seed
entities.abode: By the bank of the river Veh Daiti
entities.bio: White as the moon, killed in the first attack - and everything useful grew out of the corpse.
entities.longBio: The Sole-Created Ox is made before people, white and shining, and Ahriman kills it in the assault on the good creation. That death is generative: from its body come fifty-five kinds of grain and twelve kinds of healing plant, from its seed - carried to the moon and purified there - come all the beneficial animal species, and from its fat comes the drink of immortality at the end of time. Its soul, Geush Urvan, goes up and complains to Ahura Mazda about being abandoned, and is told that a prophet will come who will protect cattle. That prophet is Zarathustra.
entities.variantTraditions: The bull's protest in Yasna 29 is one of the oldest and strangest passages in the Gathas, and reads as a genuine plea about the treatment of livestock.

entities.name: Geush Urvan
entities.role: The Soul of the Ox, who took the case of all cattle to the gods and won
entities.abode: In the presence of Ahura Mazda
entities.bio: The soul of the murdered bull went up and complained, and the answer was: we are sending you a prophet.
entities.longBio: Geush Urvan is the Soul of the Ox, and Yasna 29 is essentially a courtroom scene. The soul cries out to Ahura Mazda about the violence and cruelty it suffers on earth and demands to know who was appointed to protect it. Asha answers that there is no herdsman free of sin. Ahura Mazda names Zarathustra. The soul is unimpressed - it wanted a mighty prince and it has been given a man with a weak voice - and the hymn ends with it accepting the appointment reluctantly. A religion whose founding text opens with livestock filing a grievance is not like the others.
entities.variantTraditions: Yasna 29 is among the oldest Gathic material and its reading is difficult; the disappointed tone of the soul's response is generally agreed.

entities.name: The Saoshyant
entities.role: The future saviour, conceived from the prophet's seed kept in a lake for millennia
entities.bio: Zarathustra's seed is preserved in a lake, and a virgin bathing there will bear the one who ends the war.
entities.longBio: The Saoshyant is the world-saviour who arrives at the end of the twelve thousand years. Zarathustra's seed is kept in Lake Kansaoya, guarded by ninety-nine thousand fravashis, and a virgin who bathes in it conceives him. He raises the dead, everyone passes through the river of molten metal, evil is destroyed and the world is made new and perfect - the Frashokereti, the making wonderful. Three saviours come in sequence at thousand-year intervals, the last being the Saoshyant proper. The whole apparatus of a virgin-born saviour, resurrection and a final judgement sits here in a religion older than the ones usually credited with it.
entities.variantTraditions: How far Zoroastrian eschatology shaped Jewish, Christian and Islamic messianism is one of the long-running arguments in the history of religion; the direction of borrowing is hard to prove but the dates favour Iran.

entities.name: The Chinvat Bridge
entities.role: The bridge of the separator, which is broad for the good and a blade for the wicked
entities.bio: Not a test you take - a bridge that measures you and changes width accordingly.
entities.longBio: Three days after death the soul comes to the Chinvat Bridge, guarded by two dogs, where Mithra, Sraosha and Rashnu wait with scales. The bridge is not fixed. For the righteous it broadens to the width of nine spears and their daena meets them as a beautiful woman and leads them across to the House of Song. For the wicked it narrows to the edge of a razor, their daena meets them as a hag, and they fall into the House of Lies. Those exactly balanced go to Hamistagan, a neutral place, until the end. Nobody stays anywhere forever.
entities.variantTraditions: The bridge appears in the Gathas already, which makes it one of the oldest elements of the eschatology. The Islamic Sirat bridge is very probably descended from it.

entities.name: The Simurgh
entities.role: The great bird who raised an abandoned baby and taught a surgeon how to operate
symbols: the enormous bird with a dog's head in early art
entities.abode: A nest in the Alborz mountains, on the tree of all seeds
entities.bio: She found a white-haired baby left to die on a mountain and raised him - and his family got the bill later.
entities.longBio: The Simurgh nests on the tree that holds every seed in the world, and when she takes off the seeds scatter and the rains carry them everywhere. In the Shahnameh she is the making of a dynasty: Sam exposes his albino son Zal on a mountain, the Simurgh takes him to her nest and raises him, and when his father comes back ashamed she returns him with three feathers - burn one and she will come. Zal uses them twice: once for Rudabeh's obstructed labour, where the Simurgh dictates what is effectively a caesarean section, and once to tell Rostam how to kill Esfandiyar.
entities.variantTraditions: The earlier Senmurv is depicted as a winged creature with a dog's head; the fully avian Simurgh is later. She has no connection to the Arabic roc beyond both being large birds.

entities.name: Zarathustra
entities.role: The prophet who laughed when he was born and argued with god about cattle
domains: the reform of the old religion
entities.abode: Airyanem Vaejah, and the court of Vishtaspa
entities.bio: The first person to say there is one god and you have to choose sides - and possibly the first prophet anywhere.
entities.longBio: Zarathustra is a real person who left real poetry: seventeen hymns, the Gathas, in a language so archaic they can barely be translated. He takes the old Indo-Iranian pantheon and reorganises it around a single creator and a moral choice, demoting the daevas to demons in the process. Tradition says he laughed at his own birth instead of crying, received the revelation at thirty from Vohu Manah, was rejected for ten years, converted King Vishtaspa by curing his horse, and was murdered at seventy-seven while tending a fire. When he lived is genuinely unknown - estimates run from 1500 to 600 BC.
entities.variantTraditions: The Gathas are linguistically close to the Rigveda, which argues for the earlier dating. The traditional date of 258 years before Alexander is now generally rejected.

entities.name: Vishtaspa
entities.role: The king who converted, after the prophet cured his favourite horse
symbols: the horse whose legs were restored
entities.bio: His horse's legs withdrew into its body; Zarathustra cured it one leg per concession.
entities.longBio: Vishtaspa is the first king to adopt the new religion, which is what turns Zarathustra from a rejected preacher into the founder of a state faith. The conversion story is a negotiation: the king's favourite black horse has all four legs drawn up into its belly, and Zarathustra offers to cure it a leg at a time in exchange for four things - that the king accept the religion, that his son take up arms for it, that the queen convert, and that the courtiers who framed the prophet be named. He gets all four. In the Shahnameh he becomes Goshtasp, a considerably less admirable figure.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Vishtaspa is the same man as the father of Darius I is an old question, generally answered no on chronological grounds.

entities.name: The Fravashis
entities.role: The guardian spirits of everyone who ever lived, who ride out in armour once a year
entities.abode: With every living thing, and in the sky
entities.bio: Every person has one, they existed before you did, and they fought on the good side before you were born.
entities.longBio: A fravashi is the pre-existent higher self of a person, and everyone has one - including the unborn, the dead, and Ahura Mazda himself. Before the world was made they were asked whether they would go down and be embodied and fight, and they agreed. Their great hymn describes them riding in thousands like armoured horsemen, and they are asked for help in battle, in childbirth and for rain. During the last ten days of the year they come home and the household prepares food for them, which is still kept as Farvardigan. The winged figure on Persepolis is very probably one.
entities.variantTraditions: The identity of the Faravahar, the winged disc, is disputed - fravashi, khvarenah or Ahura Mazda himself have all been argued.

entities.name: The Khvarenah
entities.role: The royal glory: a visible radiance that leaves a king the moment he lies
symbols: the falcon that carries it away
entities.abode: On the rightful king, and nowhere else
entities.bio: It looks like light around a king, and it physically departs when he stops deserving it.
entities.longBio: Khvarenah is the glory that marks a legitimate ruler, and the crucial thing is that it can leave. When Yima lies, it flies off him in the shape of a bird, three times, and passes to others. Azhi Dahaka grabs at it and Atar fights him for it. It falls into Lake Vourukasha and Afrasiyab dives three times trying to seize it and fails. The whole Iranian theory of kingship is here: authority is conditional, visible, and revocable by heaven rather than by people. As farr it stays central in Persian political thought for two thousand years.
entities.variantTraditions: Khvarenah is the origin of the halo in later religious art by one well-supported line of argument, travelling west through Kushan and Buddhist iconography.

entities.name: Hushang
entities.role: He threw a stone at a snake, missed, and discovered fire
entities.bio: The stone missed the snake, hit rock, and struck a spark - and that is the Persian origin of fire.
entities.longBio: Hushang is Gayomard's grandson and the second king. Out walking he sees a long dark snake with smoke coming from its mouth, picks up a stone and throws it; the snake escapes but the stone strikes rock and a spark jumps out. He understands at once what he has been given, and that night is celebrated as Sadeh, a midwinter fire festival still kept in Iran. He goes on to separate iron from stone, build the first forge, dig irrigation channels and teach people to farm. He is a culture-hero in the plainest sense: everything useful starts with him.
entities.variantTraditions: Ferdowsi is careful to say the fire came from god through the accident, not from Hushang's cleverness.

entities.name: Tahmuras
entities.role: The Demon-Binder, who beat the divs and made them teach him to write
entities.bio: He defeated the demons and spared them on one condition: teach me to write.
entities.longBio: Tahmuras binds the divs - the demons of the epic - and rides one as a mount, and when he has them beaten they offer him a ransom. What they teach him is writing, in some thirty scripts, and Ferdowsi treats literacy as something extracted from the enemy under duress rather than a gift from heaven, which is an interesting position for a poet to take. He also domesticates animals, teaches shearing and spinning, and trains hawks. His epithet Div-band sticks to him permanently.
entities.variantTraditions: The Avestan Taxma Urupi rides Angra Mainyu himself as a horse for thirty years; the epic keeps the image and lowers the target.

entities.name: Jamshid
entities.role: The greatest king in the world, ruined by saying so out loud
symbols: the throne carried into the sky
the wine cup that shows the world
entities.abode: Persepolis, called the Throne of Jamshid
entities.bio: Three hundred years of paradise, and then he claimed to be god and the glory left him in three pieces.
entities.longBio: Jamshid's reign is the golden age: he divides society into classes, invents weaving, medicine, ships and the working of metals, builds baths and perfume, and abolishes death and disease so that for three hundred years nobody dies. He founds Nowruz by having demons lift his throne into the air on the first day of spring. Then he calls an assembly and declares himself god. The khvarenah leaves him in three flights, his nobles desert, and Zahhak invades. He runs for a hundred years and is caught and sawn in half. Persepolis is still called Takht-e Jamshid, his throne.
entities.variantTraditions: The Avestan Yima builds an underground refuge, the vara, to survive a killing winter - the closest thing in Iranian tradition to a flood story, and dropped from the epic.

entities.name: Zahhak
entities.role: The king with two serpents on his shoulders that had to be fed human brains
symbols: the two black snakes from his shoulders
the daily ration of two young men
entities.abode: Jerusalem in the epic, then chained in Damavand
entities.bio: The devil kissed his shoulders and snakes grew there, and they had to be fed two human brains a day.
entities.longBio: Zahhak is a foreign prince whom Ahriman persuades to murder his own father. Then Ahriman comes back as a cook, feeds him meat until he is grateful, and asks only to kiss his shoulders - and two black serpents grow there. They cannot be cut off; they grow back. A physician, Ahriman again, advises that the only remedy is to feed them human brains daily. Zahhak takes Iran and rules a thousand years, two young men killed every day, until Fereydun and the blacksmith Kaveh bring him down. He is not killed but chained inside Mount Damavand, alive, until the end of the world.
entities.variantTraditions: The cooks Armayel and Garmayel save one of each pair by substituting sheep's brains and send them to the mountains, where they become the Kurds - Ferdowsi's own etymology.

entities.name: Kaveh
entities.role: A blacksmith who lost seventeen sons, tore up the king's petition, and raised his apron as a flag
domains: the smith's apron as a banner
symbols: the leather apron on a spear
entities.abode: The forge, and the road to Fereydun
entities.bio: The most famous act of defiance in Persian literature, and it is performed by a tradesman.
entities.longBio: Zahhak's men have taken seventeen of Kaveh's eighteen sons for the serpents. When they come for the last, Kaveh goes to the palace, where the king is circulating a document attesting that he has always ruled justly, requiring signatures. Kaveh reads it, denounces it in front of the court, tears it to pieces and walks out with his son. In the street he puts his leather apron on the point of a spear and raises it, and people follow. That apron becomes the Derafsh Kaviani, the royal standard of Iran for a thousand years, jewelled and enlarged by every dynasty until the Arabs captured it.
entities.variantTraditions: The Derafsh Kaviani was real and was taken at the battle of Qadisiyyah in 636 and cut up for its jewels.

entities.name: Fereydun
entities.role: He overthrew the serpent king with a cow-headed mace and then divided the world badly
symbols: the cow Barmayeh who nursed him
entities.bio: He beat the tyrant, ruled five hundred years, and then made one decision that ruined everything after.
entities.longBio: Fereydun is hidden at birth from Zahhak and suckled by a cow, Barmayeh, whose head he later has cast onto his mace. With Kaveh's revolt behind him he takes the palace, and is stopped by an angel from killing Zahhak - he must chain him in Damavand instead. He then rules five hundred years. His error is at the end: he divides the world between three sons, giving Rome and the west to Salm, Turan and China to Tur, and Iran itself - the best portion - to the youngest, Iraj. The two elder brothers murder Iraj, and the war between Iran and Turan that follows runs through the rest of the epic.
entities.variantTraditions: Thraetaona of the Avesta is a dragon-slayer pure and simple; the three sons and the division of the world are the epic's development.

entities.name: Iraj
entities.role: Murdered by his own brothers for being given the better country
symbols: the severed head in a box
entities.bio: He offered to give up his kingdom to keep the peace, and they killed him anyway.
entities.longBio: Iraj gets Iran, and his brothers Salm and Tur cannot bear it. He goes to them alone and unarmed and offers to renounce the throne entirely rather than fight, and Tur kills him with a golden stool and a dagger, and they send his head back to their father in a box. Fereydun's grief is one of the great set pieces of the poem. The murder is the founding crime of the whole epic - Iran is named for Iraj, the war with Turan is named for Tur, and every generation afterwards inherits the feud. His grandson Manuchehr eventually avenges him.
entities.variantTraditions: Ferdowsi uses the fratricide to set up the entire Iran-Turan conflict, which occupies more of the epic than anything else.

entities.name: Salm and Tur
entities.role: The two brothers who murdered the third, and named a country by doing it
epithets: the kings of the west and the east
domains: the origin of the long war
symbols: the golden stool used as a weapon
entities.bio: Given the west and the east, they wanted the middle, and killed their brother to get it.
entities.longBio: Salm receives Rome and the west, Tur receives Turan and China, and Iraj receives Iran. The two elder brothers, envious, demand that Iraj be disinherited, and when he comes to them offering exactly that they kill him regardless - which tells you the grievance was never about territory. Manuchehr avenges Iraj a generation later and kills them both. Turan takes its name from Tur, and every Turanian king in the rest of the epic, Afrasiyab most of all, descends from him. Ferdowsi's Turanians are not caricatures; several are more honourable than the Iranians they fight.
entities.variantTraditions: Turan is a real geographical term for the lands north-east of Iran; the epic's Turanians are generally identified with Central Asian steppe peoples.

entities.name: Manuchehr
entities.role: Iraj's avenger, who killed both uncles and sent their heads home
entities.bio: Raised for one purpose, he did it, and then ruled a hundred and twenty years.
entities.longBio: Manuchehr is descended from Iraj through a daughter, raised by Fereydun for the specific purpose of revenge. He kills Tur in battle and then Salm, and sends their heads back to his great-grandfather, which closes the account opened with the box containing Iraj's head. His long reign is the setting for the rise of the house of Sam - Zal is born and raised by the Simurgh during it, and Rostam is born at its end. He is a competent, unremarkable king whose importance is that the epic's real heroes appear on his watch.
entities.variantTraditions: The Avestan Manush.chithra is a much smaller figure; the epic gives him the whole vengeance narrative.

entities.name: Sam
entities.role: The champion who exposed his own albino son on a mountain and regretted it for years
symbols: the mountain where he left the child
entities.bio: His son was born with white hair, he took it for a demon's mark, and he left the baby to die.
entities.longBio: Sam is the greatest warrior of his generation and the story attached to him is not about fighting. His son is born perfect in every way except that his hair is white, and Sam - ashamed, afraid the nobles will laugh - has the infant carried to the Alborz and abandoned. Years later he dreams of the child and rides out to find the Simurgh has raised him. He is given his son back and spends the rest of his life making it up to him. Ferdowsi does not excuse him; he lets Zal say exactly what was done to him, and Sam has no answer.
entities.variantTraditions: The exposure motif is common in Indo-European epic; what is unusual here is that the father survives, admits it, and has to live with the son.

entities.name: Zal
entities.role: Raised by a giant bird, married against everyone's advice, father of Rostam
symbols: the three feathers of the Simurgh
entities.bio: Albino, abandoned, bird-raised, and the wisest man in the epic.
entities.longBio: Zal comes down from the mountain as a young man raised by the Simurgh, with three of her feathers and instructions to burn one if he ever needs her. He wins a court contest of riddles put by the mobeds, which establishes him as clever rather than merely large. Then he falls in love with Rudabeh, daughter of Mehrab, who is descended from Zahhak - a match everyone opposes and the astrologers eventually approve because the child will be extraordinary. It is: Rostam. Zal outlives his son and most of his line, and the epic keeps returning to him as its longest-serving voice of sense.
entities.variantTraditions: The name Zal means old man, given for his white hair. Dastan, his other name, means trick or story.

entities.name: Rudabeh
entities.role: She let down her hair for Zal to climb, and he refused to use it
entities.bio: The tower, the hair, the lover below - and then he throws up a rope rather than hurt her.
entities.longBio: Rudabeh's courtship with Zal is the finest love story in the epic and the detail everyone remembers is her hair: she lets it down from the tower for him to climb, and he refuses to pull on it, throwing his lasso over a battlement instead. Both families object - she is descended from Zahhak - and the couple simply persist until the astrologers are consulted and produce a favourable answer. Her labour with Rostam nearly kills her: the child is too large, and Zal burns a Simurgh feather. The bird arrives and dictates the procedure - wine as anaesthetic, an incision in the side, the child lifted out, and a herb on the wound.
entities.variantTraditions: The caesarean passage is often cited as an early literary description of the operation, with the child named for the delivery: rost, delivered, and tan, body.

entities.name: Rostam
entities.role: The greatest hero in Persian literature, who killed his own son and could not undo it
entities.bio: Six hundred years of service to a succession of kings who mostly did not deserve him.
entities.longBio: Rostam is the centre of the epic. Delivered by caesarean, he kills a mad elephant as a child, and thereafter carries Iran on his back for six centuries - fighting the White Demon in the Seven Trials to free Kay Kavus, whom he rescues repeatedly from consequences of his own stupidity. The two things that define him are losses. He kills Sohrab at the ford without knowing him, and learns who he was as the boy is dying. And he is forced to fight Esfandiyar, kills him with the Simurgh's trick, and is cursed for it. He dies in a pit of spears dug by his own half-brother.
entities.variantTraditions: Rostam belongs to the Sistan cycle and is largely absent from Zoroastrian scripture; he may come from Saka rather than Persian tradition.

entities.name: Rakhsh
entities.role: The horse who killed a lion while his master slept and did not wake him
domains: the first of the seven trials
symbols: the roan coat with rose spots
entities.bio: The only horse in Iran that did not buckle when Rostam pressed down on its spine.
entities.longBio: Rostam tests every horse in Iran by pressing his hand on its back until its belly touches the ground, and Rakhsh is the only one that does not flinch. He is the equal of his rider and behaves like it. In the first of the Seven Trials, a lion comes on them at night while Rostam sleeps; Rakhsh kills it alone and only then wakes him, and gets told off for taking the risk. He finds water in the desert by scenting it. At the end he dies in the same pit of spears as his master, which is the correct ending for him.
entities.variantTraditions: The hero's horse as a near-equal companion is an Iranian speciality and passes into later Persian and Turkic epic.

entities.name: Sohrab
entities.role: Killed by the father he was looking for, who did not ask his name until too late
symbols: the onyx armlet his father left
entities.bio: He went to war specifically to find his father, and found him.
entities.longBio: Tahmineh bears Rostam's son after a single night and sends word that the child is a girl, to keep him. Sohrab grows enormous, learns who his father is, and raises an army with the intention of putting Rostam on the throne of Iran. At the Iranian camp the two are matched in single combat, neither knowing the other. Sohrab asks twice whether his opponent is Rostam and is lied to. He wins the first day and spares him. On the second Rostam throws him and stabs him, and only then sees the onyx armlet on his arm. Rostam sends for the king's healing elixir and Kay Kavus refuses it.
entities.variantTraditions: Matthew Arnold's Sohrab and Rustum (1853) made the story famous in English; the parallel with the Irish Cu Chulainn and Connla is often noted.

entities.name: Tahmineh
entities.role: She came to Rostam's room at night, proposed, and lied about the child to keep him
entities.bio: She wanted a child by the greatest man alive and said so directly.
entities.longBio: Rostam's horse is stolen in Samangan and he is lodged in the palace. That night Tahmineh comes to his room with a candle, tells him she has heard of him all her life, that she wants him and wants a child by him, and that she will find his horse. He marries her at once. He leaves an onyx armlet for the child - to wear on the arm if a boy, in the hair if a girl. When Sohrab is born she sends Rostam word that it was a girl, because a son would be taken from her for war. That single lie kills the boy sixteen years later.
entities.variantTraditions: Ferdowsi gives Tahmineh the initiative in the encounter without embarrassment, which is characteristic of his women.

entities.name: Kay Kavus
entities.role: The king who tried to fly to heaven on a throne pulled by eagles
symbols: the throne lifted by four eagles
entities.abode: Mount Alborz, and the throne of Iran
entities.bio: Vain, gullible, and permanently in a hole Rostam has to pull him out of.
entities.longBio: Kay Kavus is a disaster with a crown. He invades Mazandaran on a demon's advice and is blinded and imprisoned there, and Rostam performs the Seven Trials to get him out. He tries to reach heaven by tying four starved eagles to a throne with meat on poles above them; they fly until they tire and he crashes in a forest. He believes his wife Sudabeh's accusation against his own son Siyavash and puts him to an ordeal by fire. He refuses Rostam the elixir that would save the dying Sohrab. He reigns a hundred and fifty years and Ferdowsi does not soften him.
entities.variantTraditions: The flying-throne episode is one of the best-known scenes in Persian manuscript painting.

entities.name: Siyavash
entities.role: He rode through fire to prove his innocence and was murdered anyway, in exile
symbols: the wall of fire he rode through
the plant that grew from his blood
entities.bio: The purest figure in the epic, destroyed by everyone around him behaving badly.
entities.longBio: Siyavash is Kay Kavus's son, raised by Rostam. His stepmother Sudabeh propositions him, is refused, and accuses him of assaulting her. To settle it he rides through a mountain of burning wood and comes out the other side untouched - and his father, having seen it, still cannot be trusted. He makes a treaty with Turan, which Kay Kavus orders him to break; rather than break his word he goes into exile in Turan instead, marries Afrasiyab's daughter, and is beheaded there on a slander. From his blood a plant grows. His death is the grievance that drives the rest of the war.
entities.variantTraditions: Mourning rituals for Siyavash are attested in Central Asia from the pre-Islamic period and are among the oldest datable elements of the epic.

entities.name: Sudabeh
entities.role: She wanted her stepson, was refused, and accused him of the crime she had attempted
epithets: daughter of the king of Hamavaran
entities.bio: The oldest false-accusation plot in literature, and Ferdowsi's version is the cruellest.
entities.longBio: Sudabeh has Siyavash brought to the women's quarters, propositions him, and is refused twice. She then tears her own clothes and accuses him of attacking her, and produces a stillborn child claimed as the miscarriage he caused - a substitution that is exposed and which she survives anyway, because Kay Kavus cannot bear to lose her. Siyavash's fire ordeal clears him and she remains at court, and he leaves for Turan and his death. Rostam kills her afterwards with his own hand. The story type is Potiphar's wife, Phaedra and Hippolytus, and Ferdowsi's telling is the least forgiving of the three.
entities.variantTraditions: Ferdowsi's women are more often admirable than not, and Sudabeh stands out precisely because she is an exception.

entities.name: Kay Khosrow
entities.role: The perfect king, who avenged his father, won everything, and then walked into the snow
symbols: the cup that shows the whole world
entities.abode: Iran, then out of the world
entities.bio: He achieved everything a king could, feared what it might do to him, and left.
entities.longBio: Kay Khosrow is Siyavash's son by Afrasiyab's daughter, smuggled out of Turan and raised in secret. He becomes the ideal king the epic has been waiting for: just, restrained, and finally victorious in the long war, killing Afrasiyab himself and avenging his father. Then he does something no other king does. Fearing that success will corrupt him as it corrupted Jamshid, he appoints a successor, takes leave of his nobles, and walks up into the mountains. Several who follow him are lost in a snowstorm. He is not said to die - the epic simply stops following him.
entities.variantTraditions: Kay Khosrow is Kavi Haosravah in the Avesta and is one of the figures expected to return at the end of the world in Zoroastrian eschatology.

entities.name: Afrasiyab
entities.role: King of Turan for centuries, Iran's great enemy, and not a monster
symbols: the lake he dived into after the glory
entities.bio: The villain of the epic, given more depth than most of its heroes.
entities.longBio: Afrasiyab descends from Tur and fights Iran for most of the poem. He is genuinely dangerous - a capable general and a sorcerer - and genuinely conflicted: he takes Siyavash in as a son-in-law and treats him well before being talked into killing him, and he regrets it afterwards. He dives three times into Lake Vourukasha trying to seize the royal glory and it eludes him every time, which is the Avesta's judgement on him in one image. Kay Khosrow finally hunts him down, and he is killed after a long pursuit. Ferdowsi allows him a real death scene.
entities.variantTraditions: The Avestan Frangrasyan is a straightforward villain; the epic's Afrasiyab is one of Ferdowsi's most developed characters.

entities.name: Esfandiyar
entities.role: Invulnerable everywhere except his eyes, and killed there by a tamarisk arrow
domains: obedience to a father who wants him dead
entities.bio: His father kept promising him the throne and kept inventing one more task first.
entities.longBio: Esfandiyar is made invulnerable by Zarathustra, with his eyes the single exception because they were closed when the blessing was given. He performs his own Seven Trials, spreads the faith by the sword, and is repeatedly promised the crown by his father Goshtasp, who has no intention of giving it up and keeps setting him further tasks. The last is to bring Rostam back in chains. Both men know it is wrong and neither can refuse; they fight, and Rostam, losing, burns a Simurgh feather. The bird tells him where to find a tamarisk and how to make the arrow. He shoots Esfandiyar through both eyes.
entities.variantTraditions: Rostam is cursed for the killing and dies not long after, so the episode ends the heroic age of the epic on both sides at once.

entities.name: Goshtasp
entities.role: The king who accepted the new religion and would not give his son the throne
domains: the death of his own son
symbols: the crown he would not surrender
entities.bio: Zoroastrianism's royal patron in scripture, and in the epic a father who sends his son to die.
entities.longBio: Goshtasp is the Shahnameh's version of Vishtaspa, and Ferdowsi does something uncomfortable with him. In scripture he is the king who accepts the true religion and makes it the faith of the realm, which the epic keeps. But it adds his treatment of Esfandiyar - promise after promise of the throne, each followed by another impossible errand, until he sends him against Rostam knowing what will happen. The poem's judgement is unmistakable: he gets his son killed rather than abdicate. It is one of the sharpest things in the epic, aimed at a figure the official religion revered.
entities.variantTraditions: Ferdowsi wrote for a Muslim court about Zoroastrian kings, and his freedom to criticise a scriptural figure is worth noticing.

entities.name: The White Demon
entities.role: The demon of Mazandaran, whose liver cured an army's blindness
epithets: the chief of the demons of Mazandaran
symbols: the white hair and black body
entities.bio: He blinded a whole Iranian army, and the cure was his own liver.
entities.longBio: The White Demon is the strongest of the divs of Mazandaran. He defeats Kay Kavus's invasion and strikes the king and his army blind, and it is to undo this that Rostam performs the Seven Trials. The last of them is the demon itself: Rostam finds it asleep in a cave, wakes it - refusing to strike a sleeping enemy - and they wrestle. Rostam tears off a leg, then kills it and takes the liver, and blood from it restores the sight of the king and his men. Persian miniature painters returned to the cave fight more than to almost any other scene.
entities.variantTraditions: Divs in the epic are a mixed category - sometimes demons, sometimes read as hostile hill peoples described in demonic terms.

entities.name: Akvan Div
entities.role: The demon who picked up a sleeping Rostam, ground and all, and asked him a trick question
symbols: the piece of earth lifted whole
entities.abode: The plain, and the air above it
entities.bio: Throw me in the sea or on the mountain? Rostam knew the answer was to say the opposite.
entities.longBio: Akvan appears as a whirlwind and carries off horses. When Rostam sleeps, the demon cuts out the whole patch of ground he is lying on and lifts it into the air, then offers him a choice: to be thrown into the sea or onto the mountains. Rostam knows a demon does the reverse of what it is asked, so he says the mountains, and is thrown into the sea, where he can swim. He gets out and kills it. It is a small, sharp episode and one of the few times the epic's strongest man wins by thinking rather than by force.
entities.variantTraditions: The Akvan episode is a self-contained tale sometimes treated as a later insertion into the Rostam cycle.

entities.name: Bizhan and Manizheh
entities.role: He was thrown down a pit for loving the enemy king's daughter, and she begged in the streets to feed him
symbols: the covered pit sealed with a boulder
the ring dropped in the water
entities.bio: The best-loved romance in the epic, and the woman does almost all of the work.
entities.longBio: Bizhan, an Iranian hero, meets Manizheh, Afrasiyab's daughter, at a festival across the border, and she drugs him and carries him into her father's palace. Discovered, he is thrown into a covered pit under a great stone and she is stripped of everything and driven out. She survives by begging and passes food down to him for months. Kay Khosrow finds him in the world-revealing cup, and Rostam comes disguised as a merchant; Manizheh recognises the ring he drops into her water jug. Rostam lifts the stone. She comes back to Iran with them and is received honourably.
entities.variantTraditions: The Bizhan and Manizheh episode is told by Ferdowsi as a story his wife recites to him by candlelight, one of the few personal frames in the poem.

entities.name: Gordafarid
entities.role: She fought Sohrab in armour, and when her helmet came off she talked her way out
epithets: the defender of the White Castle
entities.bio: The only person to fight Sohrab to a standstill and then beat him again with words.
entities.longBio: When Sohrab's army reaches the White Castle and the Iranian champion is killed, Gordafarid puts on armour, hides her hair under a helmet and rides out. She fights Sohrab with arrows, then with a lance, and holds him; he catches her at last and pulls off her helmet, and her hair falls out. Astonished, he presses his suit. She talks - suggesting terms, flattering him, promising the castle - and rides back through the gate, which shuts behind her. From the wall she tells him exactly what she thinks of him. The castle is evacuated overnight through a tunnel.
entities.variantTraditions: Ferdowsi's epic contains several warrior women; Gordafarid is the most famous and remains a common Iranian given name.

entities.name: Bahram Gur
entities.role: A Sasanian king remembered for hunting onagers, music, and a very bad day with a harpist
entities.bio: He proved a throne claim by taking the crown from between two lions, and he is real.
entities.longBio: Bahram Gur is a historical Sasanian king, Bahram V, and with him the Shahnameh moves from myth into recorded history without changing gear. He claims the throne by placing the crown between two lions and inviting his rival to fetch it; he takes it himself. His epithet comes from his passion for hunting the wild ass. The famous scene has him showing off to a favourite slave girl by pinning a gazelle's hoof to its ear with an arrow, and her unimpressed reply that it is practice, not skill - after which he tries to have her killed. He also imports thousands of Indian musicians.
entities.variantTraditions: The later section of the Shahnameh covers the Sasanians with reasonable historical fidelity, drawing on lost Middle Persian chronicles.

entities.name: Khosrow and Shirin
entities.role: A king, an Armenian princess, and the stonemason who loved her and lost
symbols: the milk channel cut through rock
entities.abode: Ctesiphon, and the rock of Bisotun
entities.bio: The great Persian love story, and the mason cutting a mountain is the part everyone remembers.
entities.longBio: Khosrow II falls in love with Shirin from a description before ever seeing her, and the courtship runs for years through wars, misunderstandings and separations. The part that took hold is not theirs: Farhad, a stonemason, also loves Shirin, and Khosrow sets him to cut a channel through Mount Bisotun for milk to flow, expecting it to be impossible. Farhad nearly finishes it. Khosrow sends a false message that Shirin has died, and Farhad throws himself from the rock. Khosrow's reign ends with the empire exhausted, and the Arab conquest follows within a generation.
entities.variantTraditions: Nezami's twelfth-century romance made the story famous; Ferdowsi's version is shorter and Farhad is a minor figure in it.
